questions.prompt: You override equals() in a class used as a HashMap key but not hashCode(). What is the likely result?
options: Two equal keys can land in different buckets, so lookups with an equal-but-different instance fail
HashMap falls back to equals only
questions.explanation: The contract requires that equal objects have equal hash codes. HashMap uses hashCode to choose a bucket before calling equals, so equal keys with different hashes are never compared.

questions.prompt: Why does Effective Java advise favouring composition over inheritance for classes not designed for extension?
options: Subclasses depend on the superclass's implementation details (self-use of overridable methods), which can break them when the superclass changes
questions.explanation: The classic example is an InstrumentedHashSet overriding add and addAll, where addAll internally calls add and double-counts. Wrapping the set and forwarding calls avoids depending on such internals.

questions.prompt: Given void f(Object o) and void f(String s), which is called by: Object x = "hi"; f(x);
options: f(String) because the runtime type is String
f(Object) because overload resolution uses the static (compile-time) type
questions.explanation: Overloading is resolved at compile time from declared types. Overriding is resolved at runtime by the receiver's actual class (dynamic dispatch).

questions.prompt: What does a Java record automatically provide?
options: Private final fields, a canonical constructor, accessors, and equals/hashCode/toString based on the components
questions.explanation: Records are transparent carriers of immutable data. Shallow immutability only: a List component can still be mutated unless you copy it in a compact constructor.

questions.prompt: What are HashMap's default initial capacity and load factor?
questions.explanation: With 16 buckets and load factor 0.75, the table doubles once size exceeds 12. Resizing rehashes entries into the larger table.

questions.prompt: What usually happens if you call list.remove(item) on an ArrayList while iterating it with for-each?
options: ConcurrentModificationException is thrown (fail-fast iterator), on a best-effort basis
questions.explanation: The iterator detects that modCount changed. Use iterator.remove() or list.removeIf(predicate) instead. The fail-fast check is best-effort, not a guarantee.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of get/put in a TreeMap, and what does it offer that HashMap doesn't?
options: O(log n); sorted keys with navigation methods like floorKey and ceilingKey
questions.explanation: TreeMap is a red-black tree. Use it when you need ordering or range queries; use LinkedHashMap when you need insertion or access order.

questions.prompt: What happens on List.of(1, 2, 3).add(4)?
questions.explanation: List.of returns an unmodifiable list. It also rejects null elements with a NullPointerException.

questions.prompt: According to PECS, which parameter type should a method use to read Numbers from a collection passed in?
questions.explanation: Producer Extends, Consumer Super. A List<? extends Number> can hand you Numbers (it produces). To add Numbers into a collection, use ? super Number.

questions.prompt: Why can't you write new T[] or instanceof List<String> in Java?
options: Type erasure: generic type arguments are not available at runtime
Arrays don't support generics in Java 21
questions.explanation: The compiler erases type parameters to their bounds, so the runtime has no T or String type argument. Workarounds are passing a Class<T> or using a List instead of an array.

questions.prompt: What does try-with-resources guarantee?
options: Each AutoCloseable resource is closed in reverse declaration order, even when the body throws
Resources are closed only on success
questions.explanation: If close() also throws, that exception is attached to the primary one as a suppressed exception (getSuppressed()) rather than replacing it.

questions.prompt: Which statement about checked exceptions is correct?
options: They must be declared or caught; they extend Exception but not RuntimeException
They can only be thrown by the JVM
questions.explanation: IOException is checked. IllegalArgumentException is unchecked (a RuntimeException). Error subclasses such as OutOfMemoryError are also unchecked.

questions.prompt: A try block executes return 1; and its finally block executes return 2;. What does the method return?
questions.explanation: A return in finally overrides the try block's return, and also swallows any exception in flight. That is why returning from finally is considered a bug.

questions.prompt: What happens when you build list.stream().filter(...).map(...) without a terminal operation?
options: All elements are filtered and mapped immediately
Nothing executes; intermediate operations are lazy until a terminal operation runs
questions.explanation: Streams build a pipeline and execute it on a terminal operation such as collect, forEach or count. Laziness also enables short-circuiting with findFirst and limit.

questions.prompt: What happens if you call a terminal operation twice on the same Stream instance?
options: IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed
questions.explanation: Streams are single-use. Create a new stream from the source each time, or use a Supplier<Stream<T>>.

questions.prompt: Collectors.toMap(keyFn, valueFn) encounters two elements with the same key. What happens?
options: The values are put in a list
questions.explanation: Provide a merge function, toMap(k, v, (a, b) -> a), to resolve duplicates, or use groupingBy for one-to-many.

questions.prompt: Why does ConcurrentHashMap reject null keys and values, unlike HashMap?
options: With concurrent access, get() returning null would be ambiguous (absent vs mapped to null) and can't be resolved atomically with containsKey
questions.explanation: In a single-threaded map you can call containsKey afterwards. Under concurrency the map may change between the two calls. Doug Lea has explained this ambiguity as the reason.

questions.prompt: Two threads run: if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v); on a ConcurrentHashMap. What's the problem and the fix?
options: No problem; CHM makes it atomic
Check-then-act race: both may put. Use putIfAbsent or computeIfAbsent
questions.explanation: Individual CHM operations are thread-safe, but sequences of them are not atomic. computeIfAbsent performs the check and the insert atomically for that key.

questions.prompt: What does declaring a field volatile guarantee?
options: Visibility and ordering: a write happens-before every subsequent read of that field
That the field is never cached in RAM
questions.explanation: volatile doesn't make count++ atomic, because that is a read-modify-write. Use AtomicInteger or LongAdder for counters.

questions.prompt: Thread A locks X then Y; thread B locks Y then X. Which change reliably prevents the deadlock?
options: Acquire locks in a single global order in every thread
Use volatile on X and Y
questions.explanation: Consistent lock ordering removes the circular wait. Alternatives are tryLock with a timeout (ReentrantLock) or avoiding nested locks.

questions.prompt: Java 21 virtual threads are best suited for which workload?
options: High-concurrency, I/O-bound tasks that spend most of their time blocked
questions.explanation: A virtual thread unmounts from its carrier while blocked on I/O, so you can have huge numbers of them cheaply. CPU-bound work gains nothing, because carriers are still limited to the available cores.

questions.prompt: Where do Java objects created with new normally live, and where do local primitive variables live?
options: Objects on the heap; locals in the thread's stack frame
Objects on the stack; locals on the heap
questions.explanation: Each thread has its own stack of frames holding locals and references, while objects are allocated on the shared heap. The JIT may scalar-replace non-escaping objects (escape analysis), but the language model is heap allocation.

questions.prompt: Generational garbage collectors rely on which observation?
options: Most objects die young, so collecting the young generation frequently is cheap and effective
questions.explanation: This is the weak generational hypothesis. Young collections copy the few survivors, and long-lived objects are promoted to the old generation.

questions.prompt: Java has garbage collection. How can a Java program still leak memory?
options: Objects stay reachable unintentionally, e.g. growing static collections, caches without eviction, unremoved listeners, ThreadLocals on pooled threads
questions.explanation: The GC only frees unreachable objects. Find the reference chain with a heap dump, e.g. Eclipse MAT dominator trees.

questions.prompt: Under the Java Memory Model, which pair establishes a happens-before relationship?
options: Two reads of a plain field
Unlocking a monitor and a subsequent lock of the same monitor
questions.explanation: Other happens-before edges include a volatile write followed by a read of the same field, Thread.start(), Thread.join(), and actions within one thread in program order.

questions.prompt: You have CompletableFuture<User> and a method fetchOrders(User) returning CompletableFuture<List<Order>>. Which combinator avoids nesting?
questions.explanation: thenApply would produce CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<List<Order>>>. thenCompose flattens it, much like flatMap.

questions.prompt: supplyAsync(supplier) without an executor runs where by default, and why can that hurt blocking I/O?
options: A new thread per task; too many threads
ForkJoinPool.commonPool(); blocking calls tie up its small, shared, CPU-sized pool
The caller thread; it blocks the caller
A virtual thread; there's no issue
questions.explanation: Pass a dedicated executor for blocking work. On Java 21 that could be Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().

questions.prompt: What does CompletableFuture.allOf(f1, f2, f3) return?
options: A list of the three results
A CompletableFuture<Void> that completes when all of them complete
An exception if any is slow
questions.explanation: Read the individual results afterwards with join() on each future. If any future fails, the allOf future completes exceptionally.
